newsitem.title: CANADA: Canadian defense minister leaves under cloud.
newsitem.headline: Canadian defense minister leaves under cloud.

text.p: Canadian Prime Minister Jean Chretien abruptly forced the resignation on Friday of his beleaguered defense minister, David Collenette, ostensibly for having inappropriately interfered with an immigration case.

Chretien said he was extremely sorry to accept the resignation of his long-time friend and political ally but added: "I told him that I hope soon I'll be in a position to take him back into my Cabinet."

The two main opposition parties, the Bloc Quebecois and Reform Party, suggested Chretien and his Liberals were just trying to deflect criticism temporarily of a minister who had been in hot water over what has become known as the Somalia Affair.

"This is a smokescreen," Reform defense spokesman Jim Hart said. "I think all Canadians know the reason why the defense minister has really resigned, and that is because of the mismanagement that he has had in his department."

The opposition had criticized Collenette in connection with an alleged cover-up of an incident during a peacekeeping mission several years ago in which Canadian soldiers tortured and killed several Somalis.
In the affair, Collenette had backed Chief of Defense Staff Gen. Jean Boyle even after he admitted breaking the spirit of Canada's access to information laws regarding the incident.

But Collenette told a news conference that his resignation had nothing to do with Somalia and solely to do with having breached Chretien's Cabinet guidelines by having written a letter asking for quick action on an immigration case.
"It's the only honorable thing to do," said Collenette, a long-time political ally of Chretien's.
Chretien had won a landslide election in 1993 from the Conservatives, partly because of voter frustration with scandals under former Prime Minister Brian Mulroney.
But Collenette, who said he would stay in Parliament and seek re-election, was now Chretien's third minister to step down in controversy.
Deputy Prime Minister Sheila Copps resigned in May from the cabinet and Parliament over a broken tax promise but was brought back into cabinet after winning a special election.
In January Chretien pushed aside another much-criticized official, Canadian Heritage Minister Michel Dupuy, who had written on behalf of a constituent to the agency that regulates broadcasters.
Collenette's resignation came about only because of a private request under Canada's Access to Information law.
Collenette said Chretien's chief of staff, Jean Pelletier, informed him that the letter he wrote in March to the Immigration and Refugee Board was to be released.

"I have...been informed that this letter breached the draft guidelines which you have provided to ministers concerning communications between members of the cabinet and quasi-judicial bodies," Collenette wrote Chretien.
Collenette was replaced by Human Resources Development Minister Douglas Young, who first won recognition as transport minister for selling off government agencies.
Minister of International Cooperation Pierre Pettigrew replaced Young, and the Liberal whip in the House of Commons, Don Boudria, replaced Pettigrew.
Boyle, appointed by Collenette, remained in his post, but the opposition continued to call for his resignation.
